In addition to these two basic tones, there is also a phonologically significant Downstep (Ds = !); i.e., the non-predictable lowering of H following another H ... Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages. [p.55] ... it is difficult to find any true evidence for stress, at least in the sense proposed by Ward[32]. [fn.32] This is not to assert that there is no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages. There is likely some sort phrasal stress, and also the juncture between elements of compound words appears to be marked by stress, but these are clearly not what Ward was referring to. new_statements.rule_in_words: The Lower Cross languages (a sample that explicitly includes Itu Mbon Uso) are two-tone (H, L) terraced-level tone languages with contrastive downstep; Connell finds no real evidence for word-level (lexical/root) stress and treats them as non-stress languages, allowing only probable phrase-level stress and stress-marked juncture in compounds.
new_statements.exceptions: Possible phrasal stress; juncture between elements of compound words 'appears to be marked by stress'; Faraclas (1984b) analyses Obolo (a sister language) with phrasal stress and an extra-high tone; p.104 notes positional consonant weakening in Ibibio that 'may be related to stress... an area of Ibibio phonology which to date remains unstudied'.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level (Lower Cross) statement argued mainly from Efik, Ibibio and Oro data; Itu Mbon Uso is in the thesis's 19-language sample but is not discussed individually for prosody. Word-level stress denied; phrase-level stress conceded as likely. Tone statements refer to lexical items in citation form.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is a group-level characterization of the Lower Cross languages in Connell's 1991 thesis, whose 19-language sample explicitly includes 'ItuMbuso (Itu Mbon Uso - Akwa Ibom)' (= itum1245, ISO itm); the stress argument itself is made on Efik (efik1245), Ibibio (ibib1240) and Oro (oroo1241) data and generalized to 'the other LC languages'. The only Itu Mbon Uso-specific phonology paper (Edo & Akpan 2020, consonants) is silent on stress and tone.

sources.note: Only language-specific phonological description found: 17 phonemic / 20 phonetic consonants, distribution, nasalization, palatalization (Ibadan 400 wordlist, 8 speakers). Examples are tone-marked but there is no tone or stress section; the words 'stress' and 'tone' do not occur. Silent on stress.
